regions.text: in a terrible accident on the ground.
regions.explanation: From 31.12s to 32.43s (“in a terrible accident on the ground.”), articulation rate was 8.40 syll/s against 5.88 syll/s in the reference (+43%); that is 1.1× the reference speaker's natural word-to-word variation. Faster articulation compresses the stressed syllables and the micro-pauses listeners use to segment phrases, so key words lose emphasis and comprehension drops. Fix: Slow to the reference pace here and let the pauses between clauses breathe.

From 44.72s to 45.89s (“were aware of the dangers,”), loudness relative to the speaker's own level fell 9.0 dB below the reference, bottoming out 11.4 dB down; that is 1.8× the reference speaker's natural word-to-word variation. The loudness falls away across the phrase, so its final words - often the payoff - drop toward the noise floor of the room. Fix: Support the breath through the end of the phrase; the last words need the same energy as the first.

regions.text: heroes: Michael Smith, Dick Scobee, Judith Resnik, Ronald McNair, Ellison Onizuka, Gregory Jarvis, and Christa
regions.explanation: From 51.00s to 61.92s (“heroes: Michael Smith, Dick Scobee, Judith Resnik, Ronald …”), pitch range (10th–90th percentile) narrowed to 1.2 st from 3.4 st (-66%); that is 3.2× the reference speaker's natural word-to-word variation. Pitch movement is the main cue English listeners use to find the focus word of a phrase; with a flattened contour every word carries equal weight and the line sounds recited. Fix: Lift pitch on the focus word of each clause and let it fall at the end of the thought.
